children.value: is the branch of acoustics that converts sound into electrical signals and back again, through microphones, loudspeakers, and amplifiers. It underpins nearly all modern music making, recording, and reproduction. It is also where sound crosses from the physical world into numbers, and every choice in a microphone or converter (sample rate, bit depth, codec) decides what survives that crossing.
The field of electroacoustics began in the late nineteenth century.
’s telephone (1876) showed that speech could be turned into an electrical signal and sent down a wire.

’s phonograph (1877) showed that sound could be recorded and played back mechanically. The carbon microphone, the vacuum tube amplifier, and the moving-coil loudspeaker, all developed in the early twentieth century, made electrical sound reproduction practical. Recording turned fleeting performances into objects that could be repeated, sold, and studied, and amplification let a quiet voice fill a hall;
traces how such changes reshaped the music itself. In the terms of the
, recording moved experience out of time: a perceiver no longer needs to be in the same room as the performer, or in the same year.

The condenser microphone arrived in the 1920s. Magnetic recording, FM radio, and high-fidelity audio in the mid-twentieth century then transformed music production and broadcasting. Today the field keeps changing through digital signal processing, microelectronics, and wireless transmission.
Electroacoustics is a subdiscipline of acoustics, alongside the room and instrument acoustics we met in
. The physics of sound propagation is the same, but electroacoustics adds electrical and electronic phenomena that shape how sound is captured, modified, transmitted, and reproduced.

Every recorded piece of music has passed through microphones, amplifiers, and loudspeakers, and the character of those devices shapes the timbre we hear. Live performance leans on the same equipment. In concert halls and clubs, the choice and placement of microphones and speakers decides how a performance reaches the audience. The two transducers in this chain are the microphone (acoustic to electrical) and the loudspeaker (electrical to acoustic). The stages between them, preamplifier, signal processing, and power amplifier, work entirely in the electrical domain.
Different transducers use different physical effects to convert energy:
: a conductor moving in a magnetic field generates a current. Used in dynamic microphones and moving-coil loudspeakers.
: when the distance between two charged plates changes, so does the voltage across them. Used in condenser microphones and electrostatic loudspeakers.
: some crystals and ceramics give off a charge when they are bent or squeezed. Used in contact microphones and some other transducers.
Each trades frequency response, sensitivity, dynamic range, and cost differently.
The three words are often used as if they meant the same thing, but they describe different levels of technology.
only says that something runs on electricity: a device that passes a current through a wire, a coil, or a lamp is electric.

means that the current is actively controlled by components such as valves, transistors, or the integrated circuits built from them. An oscillator that turns the steady current from a battery into a vibrating signal is electronic.

systems are electronic circuits that work on binary logic. Inside them a sound exists as a stream of numbers, with an analogue-to-digital converter at the input and a digital-to-analogue converter at the output, as the digital audio section below describes. The categories nest: every digital device is electronic, and every electronic device is electric, but not the other way round. An electric guitar’s pickup is electric, a Moog synthesiser is electronic (and analogue), and a laptop running a synthesiser plug-in is digital. Genuinely electric instruments, with no electronic circuit in them at all, are rare
. The next section looks at one.

The click is the moving-coil loudspeaker from later in this chapter working in its barest form. Connecting the battery sends a direct current through the voice coil, and the force between that current and the magnet pushes the cone outwards. A steady current holds the cone there in silence; the sound is made only at the moment the current changes, when the circuit is made or broken. That is why the instrument is played with paper clips, screws, and springs: dragged across the contacts they make and break the circuit many times a second, and the clicks turn into rattles and buzzes. With a little care the vibrating cone can be made to break its own contact, so that the circuit switches itself on and off and the instrument plays on its own.

is a transducer that converts acoustic pressure variations in the surrounding air into a corresponding electrical signal. The type, quality, and placement of a microphone strongly shape the character of any recording or live sound system.
is the most widely used type in live sound. Its operating principle is electromagnetic induction:
Sound waves cause a thin diaphragm to vibrate.
A voice coil attached to the diaphragm moves within the field of a permanent magnet.
This motion induces an electrical current in the coil, proportional to the velocity of the diaphragm.
Advantages: robust, tolerant of high sound pressure levels, requires no external power supply, relatively inexpensive.
Disadvantages: limited high-frequency response due to the inertia of the diaphragm and coil assembly; generally lower sensitivity than condenser microphones.
Typical examples include the Shure SM58 (vocal microphone) and Shure SM57 (instrument microphone), which are industry standards in live sound.
Figure: The Shure SM58, a classic dynamic stage microphone (photo: Iain Fergusson,
The diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor; a fixed backplate is the other.
The capacitor holds a fixed charge, from a battery or from phantom power through the cable.
Sound moves the diaphragm, which changes the distance between the plates and so the capacitance.
At constant charge, a change in capacitance gives a change in voltage. That voltage is the output.
Advantages: a flat, extended frequency response, high sensitivity, low self-noise, and both small-diaphragm (pencil) and large-diaphragm versions.
Disadvantages: it needs power (48 V phantom power or a battery), it is more fragile than a dynamic microphone, and it costs more.

Condenser microphones are the usual choice for studio recording of acoustic instruments, voices, and orchestras, since their flat response and low self-noise capture fine detail. Large-diaphragm condensers such as the Neumann U87 are a staple of professional studios.
Figure: The Neumann U87, a large-diaphragm condenser studio microphone (photo: PJ,
has a thin, corrugated metal ribbon hanging in a magnetic field:
Sound makes the ribbon vibrate in the field.
The movement induces a voltage, as in a dynamic microphone, but here the ribbon is both diaphragm and conductor.

Advantages: a smooth, natural roll-off at high frequencies, an excellent transient response, and what is often described as a warm, vintage sound. Ribbons are bidirectional by nature (a figure-8 pattern).

Disadvantages: the ribbon is fragile; the output is low, so a high-gain preamplifier is needed; wind and plosives are a problem; and some classic ribbons must not be given phantom power, although modern active ribbons require it.
Figure: The RCA 44-BX, a classic ribbon microphone from the 1930s and 40s (photo: Roadside Guitars,

are semiconductor-based transducers fabricated using integrated circuit manufacturing techniques. They are used in smartphones, laptops, hearing aids, and other consumer devices where small size matters most. Their performance has improved dramatically in recent years, and they are increasingly found in professional measurement applications as well.

(or directivity pattern) describes how sensitive a microphone is to sounds arriving from different directions. It is typically represented as a plot of sensitivity versus angle, in polar coordinates.
: equal sensitivity in all directions. Captures the full acoustic environment, including room reflections.
: most sensitive in front, least sensitive at the rear (heart-shaped pattern). The most common pattern for live sound and studio recording. Offers some rejection of unwanted sounds from behind.
: narrower front pickup than cardioid, with a small rear lobe. More directional; useful in noisy environments.
: picks up equally from front and rear, with strong rejection from the sides. Used in ribbon microphones and as a component in mid-side recording techniques.

In practice, polar patterns vary with frequency. Most directional microphones are more omnidirectional at low frequencies and become more directional as frequency increases. The plots below illustrate idealised patterns.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,

    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,

freq = np.logspace(np.log10(20), np.log10(20000), 1000)

def smooth_step(x, x0, width):
    """Logistic-style smooth transition centred on x0."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(x - x0) / width))

# Simulate idealised frequency responses (in dB, relative to 1 kHz)

# Dynamic: slight presence peak ~5 kHz, high-frequency roll-off above 12 kHz
dynamic = (
    2.5 * np.exp(-((np.log10(freq) - np.log10(5000)) ** 2) / (2 * 0.15 ** 2))
    - 6 * smooth_step(np.log10(freq), np.log10(12000), 0.15)
)

# Condenser: very flat, small presence peak ~10 kHz, slight HF extension
condenser = (
    1.5 * np.exp(-((np.log10(freq) - np.log10(10000)) ** 2) / (2 * 0.2 ** 2))
    - 2 * smooth_step(np.log10(freq), np.log10(18000), 0.1)
)

# Ribbon: warm roll-off starting around 8 kHz
ribbon = (
    -0.5 * np.log10(freq / 1000)
    - 4 * smooth_step(np.log10(freq), np.log10(8000), 0.2)
)

# Low-frequency roll-off common to most mics (high-pass due to housing)
lf_rolloff = -10 * smooth_step(-np.log10(freq), -np.log10(80), 0.15)

dynamic   += lf_rolloff
condenser += lf_rolloff
ribbon    += lf_rolloff

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.semilogx(freq, dynamic,   label='Dynamic (moving-coil)', color='steelblue',  linewidth=2)
ax.semilogx(freq, condenser, label='Condenser (capacitor)',  color='darkorange', linewidth=2)
ax.semilogx(freq, ribbon,    label='Ribbon',                 color='seagreen',   linewidth=2)
ax.axhline(0, color='grey', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8, label='0 dB reference')
ax.set_xlim(20, 20000)
ax.set_ylim(-15, 8)
ax.set_xlabel('Frequency (Hz)')
ax.set_ylabel('Relative level (dB)')
ax.set_title('Idealised Frequency Responses of Microphone Types')
ax.set_xticks([50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000])
ax.set_xticklabels(['50', '100', '200', '500', '1k', '2k', '5k', '10k', '20k'])
ax.grid(True, which='both', alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()

its frequency response is, how quiet it is when nothing is happening (

Output voltage for a given sound pressure level (usually 1 Pa / 94 dB SPL). Higher (less negative) is more sensitive.

The specification sheet is only half the story, though. Engineers do not choose an SM58 or a U87 because one is “better”; they choose a sound. Microphones colour what they capture, and those colours have become part of music history: the crooner’s intimacy is a sensitive microphone up close, and much of what we recognise as the sound of a favourite record is a chain of such choices. Reading a specification sheet tells you what a microphone can do; listening through it tells you what it does to the music.

Look up the specifications of two microphones: one dynamic (e.g., Shure SM58) and one condenser (e.g., Neumann U87). Compare their self-noise, maximum SPL, and frequency response. For what recording situations would each be better suited?
converts electrical signals into acoustic pressure variations. It is the final electroacoustic transducer in most audio reproduction systems.
is by far the most common loudspeaker type. Its operation is the electromagnetic inverse of the dynamic microphone:
An alternating electrical current flows through a voice coil suspended in a permanent magnetic field.
The interaction of the current and the magnetic field produces a force on the coil (Lorentz force), causing it to move back and forth.
The coil is attached to a cone (diaphragm), whose movement creates pressure waves in the surrounding air.
Most practical loudspeaker systems use several drivers, each optimised for a different frequency range:
: handles low frequencies (bass), typically 20–500 Hz. Large diameter cone (15–40 cm) for efficient low-frequency radiation.
: covers middle frequencies (500 Hz – 5 kHz), where much of the energy of speech and music is concentrated.
: handles high frequencies (5–20 kHz). Small diameter diaphragm (2–4 cm) for extended high-frequency response.
: dedicated low-frequency driver (20–200 Hz) for cinema, music production, and concert sound reinforcement.
routes the appropriate frequencies to each driver, ensuring that each operates within its optimal range.

Most headphones use dynamic (moving-coil) drivers; high-end models may use planar magnetic or electrostatic elements. Headphones bypass the room and the pinnae, so they sound different from loudspeakers and can change the perceived spatial image. That makes them attractive for controlled listening experiments in music psychology. It also means that a mix made on headphones may sound different over loudspeakers.

# Active noise cancellation: a second sound in opposite phase cancels the first, as long as the timing is exact.
fs = 48000
t = np.arange(0, 0.012, 1 / fs)
noise = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 120 * t) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 310 * t)
anti = -noise
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
for k, (y, label, col) in enumerate([(noise, "noise", "C0"), (anti, "anti-noise (same sound, opposite phase)", "C1"), (noise + anti, "sum at the ear: silence", "C2")]):
    ax0.plot(t * 1000, y - 3.2 * k, color=col, lw=1.5)
    ax0.text(0, 1.6 - 3.2 * k, label, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax0.set_yticks([]); ax0.set_xlabel("Time (ms)"); ax0.set_title("Adding the opposite phase")
ax0.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
f = np.logspace(1, 4, 300)
for delay_us, col in [(10, "C0"), (50, "C1"), (200, "C2")]:
    residual = 20 * np.log10(np.maximum(2 * np.abs(np.sin(np.pi * f * delay_us * 1e-6)), 1e-6))   # remaining level, dB re the noise
    ax1.plot(f, residual, color=col, lw=1.5, label=f"timing error {delay_us} µs")
ax1.axhline(0, color="0.5", ls="--", lw=1); ax1.text(12, 1, "no reduction", fontsize=8, color="0.4")
ax1.set_xscale("log"); ax1.set_ylim(-45, 8); ax1.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)"); ax1.set_ylabel("Remaining noise (dB)")
ax1.set_title("Why cancellation works best at low frequencies"); ax1.legend(loc="lower right")

Figure: Active noise cancellation. Left: a noise, the same sound in opposite phase, and their sum, which is silence. Right: cancellation only works if the anti-noise arrives at exactly the right moment; the curves show how much noise remains when the timing is off by 10, 50, and 200 microseconds. A 200 µs error still removes most of a 100 Hz hum but nothing at 1 kHz, which is why noise-cancelling headphones silence engines and ventilation and leave voices alone.

Headphone listening also deserves a moment of reflection. For most people today, most music arrives through earbuds. This is a private, portable listening situation, completely different from how music has been experienced throughout human history. The sound appears inside the head rather than at a place in the room, nobody around you knows what you are hearing, and the music travels with you in changing environments and contexts. It is a very different experience from playing, listening, and moving (including dancing) together, and that difference matters when we study music and its effects.
How do you usually listen to music? How does it influence your experience?

Like microphones, loudspeakers are described by their frequency response. Unlike microphones, a single driver can hardly cover the whole audio range flat, which is why systems with several drivers and a crossover are the norm.

of a loudspeaker is the sound pressure level (in dB SPL) it produces at 1 metre when driven with 1 watt (or 2.83 V into 8 Ω). A more sensitive loudspeaker needs less amplifier power for the same level.

def bandpass_response(f, f_low, f_high, slope_low=24, slope_high=24):
    """Simulate a bandpass driver response with gentle Butterworth-like slopes."""
    low_shelf  = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + (f_low / f) ** slope_low)
    high_shelf = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + (f / f_high) ** slope_high)
    return 20 * np.log10(low_shelf * high_shelf + 1e-10)

woofer     = bandpass_response(freq, 50,   1000, slope_low=12, slope_high=12)
midrange   = bandpass_response(freq, 300,  5000, slope_low=12, slope_high=12)
tweeter    = bandpass_response(freq, 3000, 22000, slope_low=12, slope_high=24)

A loudspeaker does not operate in isolation; it interacts strongly with the room in which it is placed. Reflections from walls, floor, and ceiling combine with the direct sound at the listener’s ears, modifying the perceived frequency response and spatial character.

) make low frequencies loud in some spots and almost absent in others. Some people believe that a subwoofer can be placed anywhere. That is not true; you can easily test this by moving a subwoofer around in a room. Try to place it in a corner, then 1 metre from a wall and in the middle of the room. This will change the experienced bass sound more than any equaliser will.
A speaker close to a wall radiates more low end, because the reflection reinforces the direct sound; a corner adds more still. This is
, and it is why the same speaker sounds different once you move it.

When setting up two speakers in a stereo setup, the usual starting point is an equilateral triangle: you at one corner, the two speakers at the others tilted towards you so that the tweeters are at ear height and away from walls.

These effects mean that the same loudspeaker can sound quite different in different rooms, and that acoustic treatment of the room and careful speaker placement are as important as the choice of loudspeaker itself.

increases the power, voltage, or current of an electrical signal. Audio needs it because a microphone produces only millivolts, while a loudspeaker needs far larger voltages and currents to make audible sound.
Audio signals travel at very different strengths through the chain, and each input expects one of them. There are four, from weakest to strongest.

Signal processing is the field that analyses, modifies, and synthesises signals such as sound, images, and scientific measurements. In audio, it is how we improve sound quality, pull out information, and adapt a signal for a purpose.

It can happen in the analogue or the digital domain. The thing to remember is that everything you hear through a loudspeaker is processed, by hand or, increasingly, automatically. Filtering and equalisation shape the tone, compression evens out the dynamics, and reverberation and other effects place the sound in a real or imagined space. The same operations run in a guitar pedal, a mixing console, a phone, and a hearing aid.
Dig deeper: main uses of signal processing in audio
: increasing the strength of electrical signals so they can drive loudspeakers or be recorded at usable levels.
: removing unwanted frequencies (such as noise or hum) or enhancing desired frequency ranges. Filters can be low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or notch filters.
: adjusting the balance between frequency components to shape the tonal quality of audio signals.
: reducing the difference between the loudest and quietest parts of a signal to make audio more consistent and prevent distortion.
: techniques such as gating, spectral subtraction, or adaptive filtering to minimise background noise.
: adding reverberation, delay, chorus, distortion, or other effects to enhance or creatively alter the sound.
: changing aspects of the signal such as amplitude, frequency, or phase for transmission or synthesis.

sr = 4000                                  # coarse rate: enough to draw the shapes
def adsr(attack, decay, sustain, release, hold, sr=sr):
    """ADSR envelope; `hold` is how long the key stays down (s)."""
    a = np.linspace(0, 1, int(attack * sr), endpoint=False)
    d = np.linspace(1, sustain, int(decay * sr), endpoint=False)
    s_len = max(0, int(hold * sr) - len(a) - len(d))
    s = np.full(s_len, sustain)
    r = np.linspace(sustain, 0, int(release * sr))
    env = np.concatenate([a, d, s, r])
    return np.arange(len(env)) / sr, env

shapes = {

Things in a spectrogram that are not the sound

Some features of a spectrogram belong to the recording chain rather than to what was played. A hard ceiling at 15–16 kHz or 19.5 kHz, with nothing above it, is the low-pass filter of a lossy codec such as MP3 or AAC. A hard ceiling at half the sampling rate is the Nyquist limit of the recording itself. A uniform faint wash across the whole picture is the noise floor of the microphone and the converter. A steady band below 50 Hz is often handling noise, wind, or mains hum. Levels that drift up in quiet passages and down in loud ones are a phone’s automatic gain or an “audio enhancement” setting. Name these for what they are before you interpret them as music.

First, the continuous sound wave is measured at regular intervals, producing a stream of samples. The number of measurements per second is the

# A short "sound": a 500 Hz tone with a weaker 1500 Hz partial, 4 ms long
dur = 0.004
tt = np.linspace(0, dur, 4000)
def wave(t):
    return 0.7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 500 * t) + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1500 * t)

def quantise(x, bits):
    levels = 2 ** bits
    step = 2 / levels
    return np.clip(np.round(x / step) * step, -1, 1 - step)

rates = [32000, 8000, 4000]     # rows: samples per second

The sampling rate is the number of samples per second taken from a continuous signal to create a discrete signal. According to the
, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal to reconstruct it accurately. This minimum rate is the
; half the sampling rate, the highest frequency the system can represent, is the
. Since humans can hear frequencies up to around 20,000 Hz, this means that sound needs to be sampled at more than 40,000 Hz to capture all audible sound.

Digital audio has for a long time been standardised at 44,100 Hz, which can represent frequencies up to 22,050 Hz. The specific number is a piece of history dating back to the introduction of the CD. The rate had to be a little above twice the 20 kHz upper limit of hearing, to leave room for the anti-

filter that removes everything above the Nyquist frequency before sampling. The exact value came from video. In the late 1970s the only recorders with enough bandwidth for digital audio were video tape machines, so early systems such as Sony’s PCM adaptors stored the audio samples as a pseudo-video picture, three samples per television line. 44,100 Hz is the rate that fits a whole number of samples into both television standards: 60 fields per second × 245 usable lines × 3 samples in NTSC, and 50 × 294 × 3 in PAL, both give 44,100. When Sony and Philips finalised the CD in 1980, the mastering recorders already ran at this rate, and it has stayed with us ever since. Professional recording often uses 48 kHz, 96 kHz, or higher. Higher sampling rates can reduce aliasing, where frequencies too high to be represented reappear as false lower tones (demonstrated below), and leave more headroom for some processing tasks, but they also increase file size and CPU load.

is the number of bits used for each sample. It sets the precision of the stored amplitude: more bits give less quantisation noise and a greater dynamic range. CDs use 16 bits per sample, professional recording usually 24, and modern recorders increasingly 32-bit floating point. The headroom of 32-bit float is so large that a badly set recording level can often be rescued afterwards. At normal listening levels the audible differences are small. What the extra bits buy is a safety margin while recording and processing.
If you had to choose, would you prefer to have a higher sampling rate (e.g. 96 kHz and 16-bit) or a higher bit depth (e.g. 44.1 kHz and 32-bit)?

connects microphones, instruments, and other audio sources to a computer for recording, and routes the computer’s audio output to loudspeakers or headphones for playback. All laptops and mobile phones have built-in audio interfaces, but for professional use, it is common to have an external device that you connect with a USB cable.

Inside, an interface combines the pieces this chapter has introduced one by one: microphone preamplifiers, the analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue converters, and a headphone amplifier, connected to the computer over USB or another protocol.

The converters in an audio interface apply the principles of sampling and quantisation described above. The quality of the ADCs and DACs, together with the chosen sample rate and bit depth, affects the transparency, noise floor, and working headroom of a recording system.

In a digital audio workstation (DAW), a live performance setup, or a real-time synthesis patch, audio is processed in
(buffers) of samples rather than as one infinite stream. The buffer size, together with the sampling rate, sets how often the computer must finish a round of processing. A smaller buffer means lower

, the delay between input and output, but it leaves less time per block and raises CPU load. A larger buffer is more forgiving with heavy plug-ins, but it increases latency and can make timing feel sluggish when you monitor yourself or play virtual instruments.

Round-trip latency comes from several places: analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue conversion, buffering in the driver and the application, and the digital signal processing in the chain. Interfaces and drivers often report separate input and output figures, but what matters to a performer is the total monitoring delay. To avoid hearing themselves late, many systems offer direct monitoring, an analogue path from input to headphones that bypasses the computer.

At the University of Oslo we have researched network music performance for many years: musicians play together from different locations, which by design introduces latency. Making it work is a technical challenge, it raises psychological questions about togetherness and timing, and it can produce music of its own kind.

To decide what to remove, a lossy codec leans directly on
splits the signal into frequency bands and, moment by moment, runs a psychoacoustic model of what a human ear would actually notice. The main phenomenon is

: a strong sound makes weaker sounds close to it in frequency (simultaneous masking) or in time (temporal masking) inaudible. Components the model predicts are masked can be stored very coarsely or discarded altogether, and the saved bits are spent where hearing is most sensitive.

This is why an MP3 file at a typical streaming bitrate keeps less than a tenth of the data in the CD-quality original, yet most listeners cannot tell the difference. Push the bitrate lower and the model must start discarding components that are not fully masked, which is when the familiar artefacts appear: a swirly, underwater quality, most audible in cymbals, reverb tails, and other noise-like sounds. Lossy compression is applied psychoacoustics: it works because we do not hear everything that reaches our ears.

The ears locate a sound using three cues: the difference in arrival time between the ears, the difference in level, and the filtering the head and outer ear impose. How these cues work in perception is explained in the next chapter,
. Spatial audio is the engineering side of the same problem: delivering those cues convincingly over loudspeakers or headphones.

The oldest and still the most common approach stores one signal per loudspeaker. Stereo is the familiar case. A source panned between two speakers is not really located anywhere: sending the same signal to both at equal level produces a

, which the listener hears as coming from a point between the speakers even though nothing is radiating from there. Adjusting the balance slides the image left or right. Surround formats such as 5.1 extend the idea with more speakers, adding rear channels for ambience and a dedicated low-frequency channel.
Channel-based audio is simple and reliable, but the mix is made for one specific loudspeaker layout, and the illusion is only reliable in the
, the small region roughly equidistant from the speakers. If you move off-centre, the phantom images collapse towards whichever speaker you are nearest.
If the spatial cues are things that happen at the two eardrums, then delivering them over headphones is a matter of reproducing the right signal at each ear. That is what

Binaural audio can be convincing, but it has two well-known problems. HRTFs are individual, since they depend on the shape of your head, torso, and outer ears, so a generic HRTF localises less well for most listeners, but not all. Also, a static binaural rendering turns with your head, which the real world does not do. That is why many virtual reality (VR) systems use head trackers to rotate the auditory scene to compensate.

The third approach stores neither speakers nor ears but a description of the sound field itself, which is decoded to whatever playback system is at hand.

is the main example, a full-sphere surround technique. A first-order recording has four channels, together called B-format, which capture the overall pressure at a point and the direction the sound comes from. Higher orders add channels and sharpen the spatial resolution.

The practical appeal is that recording and reproduction are decoupled. One ambisonic recording can be decoded to headphones, to a stereo pair, or to a dome of 30 speakers, and it can be rotated before decoding. That is why it is the usual carrier format for virtual reality and 360-degree video. Because such a recording stores direction as well as level, it can also be analysed to show where sound comes from and how diffuse it is.

A fourth approach, common in cinema, stores each source as a mono signal plus metadata saying where it should be, and leaves the renderer in the playback room to work out which speakers to use. This is object-based audio, and it is best understood as deferring the panning decision from the mixing stage to the listening stage.

is the best-known example. It began in cinemas in 2012, where a mix of up to 128 objects is rendered to whatever speaker array the theatre has, including overhead speakers for height. Since the early 2020s it has also become a delivery format for music: streaming services offer Atmos mixes of albums, and on headphones these are rendered binaurally, so most listeners meet object-based audio as a form of binaural playback.

Atmos and ambisonics are easy to confuse, since both promise independence from the playback layout, but they store different things. An ambisonic recording describes the sound field at one point, sources and room together, and the decoder derives speaker or headphone feeds from that description; it can be captured directly with a microphone and rotated as a whole. Atmos stores individual sources, each a mono signal with metadata about where it should be, and the renderer places them on whatever speakers exist. That makes it a production format rather than a recording format: objects are authored in a mix, and a room cannot be recorded into Atmos the way it can with an ambisonic microphone. In practice the two often meet, as when a game or VR engine carries the ambience as ambisonics and the characters as objects, and both end up rendered binaurally on headphones.

A professional recording studio provides a controlled acoustic environment with carefully treated rooms, high-quality microphones, preamplifiers, and monitoring loudspeakers. The most consequential decision is often simply distance.

children.value: Streaming services sell tiers of sound quality, and hi-fi magazines have argued for decades that 24-bit audio at 96 or 192 kHz sounds audibly better than the 16-bit, 44.1 kHz standard of the CD. The chapter has explained what those numbers mean, which makes this a good claim to test against listening experiments.
is that the extra bandwidth above 20 kHz and the finer amplitude resolution of high-resolution formats produce an improvement that listeners can hear.

cuts both ways. In one widely cited study, a CD-quality analogue-to-digital-to-analogue loop was inserted into the playback of high-resolution recordings on high-end systems, and over more than 500 blind trials the listeners, many of them audiophiles and audio professionals, picked the right one about half the time, which is chance

. A later meta-analysis pooled 18 studies with over 12,000 trials and found a small but statistically reliable ability to tell the formats apart, a few percentage points above chance overall and clearer for listeners who had been trained on the task

in both cases is blind discrimination: the listener hears two versions and must say whether they differ, without knowing which is which. The disagreement is partly about material. Critics of the first study argued that many of its recordings had been mastered from 44.1 or 48 kHz sources and so contained nothing to hear; critics of the meta-analysis note that it pools studies with very different designs.

are the important part. Where a difference is found, it is tiny, it needs training to detect, and detecting a difference is not the same as preferring it. Mastering choices, loudspeakers, and the room change the sound far more than the format does.

The chapter’s account of sampling explains why. A 44.1 kHz rate already captures the audible range, and 16 bits with dither put the quantisation noise below the noise of any listening room. The value of higher rates and depths lies in production, where headroom and processing margin matter. Recording at 24 bits is sound engineering; paying to stream at 192 kHz is mostly buying a number.

Electroacoustics follows sound from the air into a wire and back again. Microphones and loudspeakers are the transducers at either end; preamplifiers, converters, processors, and power amplifiers work in the electrical domain between them. Each microphone type (dynamic, condenser, ribbon, MEMS) trades robustness, sensitivity, and self-noise differently, and its polar pattern and frequency response colour what it captures. Engineers therefore choose a sound rather than a specification. Loudspeakers and headphones do the reverse job, and where they sit, in a room or in the ears, shapes the result as much as the device. Signal levels and gain staging keep the chain clean, balanced connections keep it quiet, and processing (filtering, equalisation, compression, effects) touches everything we hear. Synthesisers make the signal from scratch: by subtracting from rich waveforms, adding partials, modulating frequencies, or replaying and reshaping recordings. Digital audio adds sampling and quantisation, whose rate and bit depth decide what survives the crossing into numbers; latency, perceptual codecs, and file formats follow from that. Spatial audio delivers the localisation cues over loudspeakers (channel-based), headphones (binaural), a description of the sound field (ambisonics), or sources with position data (object-based formats such as Atmos). Two reflective threads run underneath: recorded sound is split from its source (schizophonia), and every device in the chain, from the microphone to the earbuds most music is now heard through, colours the music rather than transmitting it neutrally. A critical look at high-resolution audio showed that blind tests find at most a tiny, trained difference from CD quality, and that the extra bits earn their keep in production, not playback.
